### **1649–51: The third Civil War**

The execution of Charles I was opposed by the Scots Parliament, which entered negotiations with the king’s son, Prince Charles. He was asked to agree to Presbyterian religion in England, and to sign the Covenant. Charles needed an army because Parliament had launched a new campaign in Ireland with Cromwell in command late in 1649, and all Royalist military resources were committed there. Cromwell’s success in Ireland induced Prince Charles to accept the Covenant and he arrived in Scotland in June 1650 (but was not crowned as king until 1 January 1651).

With Scotland now hostile, the English Parliament sent an army north with Cromwell in command. Initially, the Scots commander, Alexander Leslie, conducted a canny campaign of refusing pitched battle, allowing lack of supplies and disease to deplete the English force and to cause its retreat. However, when Leslie finally offered battle at Dunbar on 3 September 1650, Cromwell defeated him. After another defeat at Inverkeithing on 20 July 1651, Charles went south and assembled a combined army at Worcester.

At Worcester, a huge Parliamentarian army gathered from all over England to confront what was considered as a Scottish invasion – some 32,000 English soldiers confronted Charles’s 16,000. It was another decisive victory for Cromwell and Parliament, and though Charles escaped, the third Civil War was at an end.

Prince Charles fled the Battle of Worcester and hid in an oak tree at [Boscobel House](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/boscobel-house-and-the-royal-oak/) in Shropshire, before escaping to France disguised as the servant of a local gentlewoman, Jane Lane. ### **The impact of the wars**

The English Civil Wars were hard-fought, bloody struggles that divided society at every level, splitting individual families, villages, towns and counties across the kingdom. Although there were several large military campaigns and many medium to large battles, the war was also fought locally, in thousands of small skirmishes and sieges on small castles, towns and manor houses. People were bitterly divided, and fighting became personal and unrestrained. Countless atrocities were inflicted by soldiers, intent on the control of territory and resources to further their wider aims.

The war brought wounding, death, psychological damage, plundering and destruction on a huge scale in many areas of England. Towns and countryside were stripped of what they could supply by armies on the move or to support local garrisons. Livelihoods were lost and gained. Law and order broke down, so acts of violence and destruction went unpunished. Some groups were victimised, notably Catholics, who were vilified by the Parliamentarian side. Communities were further split by the activities of spies and informers.

It is estimated that as many as one in four adult men, from a total population of about 4.5 million people, took up arms and up to 200,000 civilians (men, women and children) and soldiers lost their lives from fighting and diseases spread by moving armies – 4.5% of the population. That was as great a loss, proportionally, as during the First World War (1914–18).

**AFTERMATH AND LEGACY**
------------------------

### **1649–60: The Commonwealth of England**

The period between 1649 and 1660 is often called the Interregnum, when no monarch ruled.

On 19 May 1649, the Rump Parliament created the Commonwealth of England. The monarchy and Privy Council were abolished and replaced by Parliament and a Council of State, the latter elected each year. However, in 1653, after four years of deliberations, England’s new leaders had not agreed on a satisfactory constitution for how the country was to be governed. In frustration and with the backing of the Army, Oliver Cromwell dissolved the Rump Parliament and organised the creation of a National Assembly. Often called the Barebones Parliament, it met for the first time on 4 July 1653, but factional in-fighting and widely differing opinions meant it achieved nothing.

At this point, backed by the Army, Cromwell dismissed Parliament and introduced a written constitution known as the Instrument of Government. At the head of government was a Lord Protector –Cromwell himself. From then on, England, Wales, Scotland, and Ireland were ruled with one government, known as the Protectorate. Three parliaments sat during the Protectorate but in between their sittings, Cromwell, his Council of State and the Army ruled.

Oliver Cromwell depicted as Lord Protector in 1653 (© The Print Collector/Print Collector/Getty Images)

Oliver Cromwell depicted as Lord Protector in 1653 (© The Print Collector/Print Collector/Getty Images)

The government of the Protectorate practised religious toleration of all Protestant sects, but persecuted Catholics, and abolished bishops. It was morally radical along Puritan lines, creating restrictions on public behaviour and events. Theatres were closed, bearbaiting and sports were banned, plain clothing was encouraged, and Christmas celebrations – beyond the religious – were outlawed.

When Cromwell died in 1658, most people had had enough of the Protectorate. Although his son Richard became Lord Protector for a while, he was unable to control the Army or Parliament, and was quietly and bloodlessly removed from power.

### **1660: The return of a king**

In May 1659, Parliament formed a Committee of Safety which led in turn to a new Council of State. But there was a power vacuum, into which stepped General George Monck, the commander of English forces in Scotland and a Royalist sympathiser. Monck allowed the moderate Presbyterian MPs removed by Pride’s Purge in 1648 to return to Parliament in February 1660.

Realising the time was right, in April 1660 Prince Charles, in exile, proclaimed the Declaration of Breda, which promised a pardon for all crimes committed during the Civil War and after to those who recognised him as king. In May, Parliament declared that Charles was the lawful successor to Charles I and began to form legislation that would bring the monarchy back. By 29 May, Charles II was in London – a king had returned.

Charles II was crowned in Westminster Abbey on 23 April 1661, restoring the monarchy to England after 11 years of Commonwealth rule (© Fine Art Images/Heritage Images via Getty Images)

Charles II was crowned in Westminster Abbey on 23 April 1661, restoring the monarchy to England after 11 years of Commonwealth rule (© Fine Art Images/Heritage Images via Getty Images)

### **The legacy**

The English Civil Wars and the Interregnum brought about the end of the monarchy, but only for 11 years. The motivations of the Parliamentarian winners were varied, and it proved impossible for them to reconcile their political, religious and social desires and agree a new constitution for government. Frustration led to a military-backed oligarchy taking over, held together largely by the will and authority of one man: Oliver Cromwell.

With its strict moral code and political in-fighting, the new government was unable to satisfy the people at large that it was a better alternative to a monarch. The failure of the regime is evident in the way it crumbled after Cromwell’s death and the ease with which a king was restored.

An allegorical engraving printed in 1683 shows the ‘ship of state’ in stormy waters with the king being thrown overboard, while Westminster stands firm (© Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

An allegorical engraving printed in 1683 shows the ‘ship of state’ in stormy waters with the king being thrown overboard, while Westminster stands firm (© Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

However, there was a political legacy. The reigns of Charles II (1660–85) and especially of James II (1685–8) witnessed continuing tension between the monarch and Parliament. James II attempted to exercise absolute authority and met with Parliamentarian opposition. He was deposed in 1688 and the new joint monarchs, William III and Mary, agreed to Parliament’s Bill of Rights in 1689, a series of measures that ensured the monarch could not suspend laws, raise taxes, make royal appointments, or maintain a peacetime army without Parliament’s permission.

These measures were the real beginning of the constitutional monarchy that we know today, in which Parliament functions as the true seat of power, but they had their roots in the Civil Wars of 1642–51.

10.content:
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| The Engagers |
| --- |
| [![Image 1: Black helmet featuring a wide brim, neck guard, and a face guard perforated with holes](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/17thC_dragoon%27s_helmet.JPG/330px-17thC_dragoon%27s_helmet.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:17thC_dragoon%27s_helmet.JPG) A Covenanter's helmet from the period in the [Museum of Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Edinburgh "Museum of Edinburgh") |
| Founded | December 1647 |
| Dissolved | 1651 |
| Split from | [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters") |
| Religion | [Presbyterianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism "Presbyterianism") ([Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland")) |
| * [Politics of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Scotland "Politics of Scotland") * [Political parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_Scotland "List of political parties in Scotland") * [Elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Scotland "Elections in Scotland") |

The **Engagers** were a faction of the [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland")[Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters"), who made "**The Engagement**" with King [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") in December 1647 while he was imprisoned in [Carisbrooke Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle") by the [English Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Parliamentarians "English Parliamentarians") after his defeat in the [First Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War").

[![Image 2: A historical document titled A Solemn League and Covenant with text detailing Reformation and defence of Religion, the Honour and happiness of the King, and the Peace and Safety of the three kingdoms of England, Scotland, and Ireland](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/The_Solemn_League_And_Covenant.jpg/250px-The_Solemn_League_And_Covenant.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Solemn_League_And_Covenant.jpg)

The [Solemn League and Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solemn_League_and_Covenant "Solemn League and Covenant") agreed by English and Scottish Presbyterians in 1643

In the 17th and 18th centuries, politics and religion were closely linked; it is impossible to understand differences between Engagers, Royalists or [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party") political views without an appreciation of these distinctions.

'[Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_polity "Presbyterian polity")' versus '[Episcopalian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_polity "Episcopal polity")' implied differences in governance, not [doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctrine "Doctrine"). Episcopalian meant rule by bishops, appointed by the monarch; Presbyterian structures were controlled by [Elders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elder_(Christianity) "Elder (Christianity)"), nominated by their congregations. Arguments over structure or governance of the church were as much about politics and the power of the monarch as religious practice; political divisions often centred on different interpretations of this.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-1)

The [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Reformation "English Reformation") created a [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland"), or 'kirk', Presbyterian in structure and governance, and predominantly [Calvinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinism "Calvinism") in doctrine. When [James VI and I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_VI_and_I "James VI and I") became king of England in 1603, a unified Church of Scotland and England governed by bishops became the first step in his vision of a centralised, Unionist state.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStephen201055%E2%80%9358-2) Although both churches were nominally Episcopalian, they were very different in doctrine; even bishops in Scotland viewed many [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") practices as little better than Catholicism.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonald199875%E2%80%9376-3)

[![Image 3: Painting of Algernon Sidney wearing armor with a white collar](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg/250px-1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg)

[James Graham, Marquis of Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquis_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquis of Montrose"); Royalist commander in Scotland 1644–1645, but a Covenanter general 1638 to 1640

Efforts by [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") to impose uniform practices led to the 1638 [National Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Covenant "National Covenant"), whose signatories pledged to resist liturgical 'innovations'. In December 1638, bishops were expelled from the kirk; when Charles attempted to use military force, he was defeated in the 1639 and 1640 [Bishops' Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops%27_Wars "Bishops' Wars"), which left the [Covenanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanter "Covenanter") party in control of Scotland.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMackieLenmanParker1986204%E2%80%93205-4)

Calvinists believed a 'well-ordered' monarchy was part of God's plan; as a result, the vast majority of Covenanters agreed monarchy itself was divinely ordered but disagreed on who held ultimate authority in clerical affairs.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacleod20095%E2%80%9319_passim-5) Royalists and Engagers tended to argue the king held supreme authority, but that did not necessarily mean they supported bishops and individual motives were very complex. Many fought for both Covenant and king at different times, including [Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquis_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquis of Montrose").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris201553%E2%80%9354-6)

When the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") began in 1642, Scotland initially remained neutral, but became involved in the [Irish Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Rebellion_of_1641 "Irish Rebellion of 1641"); the bitterness of this conflict radicalised views in Scotland and Ireland.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005142-7) The Covenanter faction known as the [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party"), led by [Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll"), saw religious union with England as the best way to preserve a Presbyterian kirk and in October 1643 the [Solemn League and Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solemn_League_and_Covenant "Solemn League and Covenant") agreed a Presbyterian Union in return for Scottish military support.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobertson2014125-8)

Royalists and moderates in both Scotland and England opposed union, as did the religious [Independents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_(religion) "Independent (religion)") like [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell"), who dominated the [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") and opposed any state-ordered church. Both Covenanters and their English allies saw the Independents as a bigger threat than the Royalists and when Charles surrendered in 1646, they began negotiations to restore him to the English throne.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005420%C2%B7423-9)

[![Image 4: Portrait of Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll, depicting a man in a black cap and dark clothing with a white collar, set against a plain background and framed within an oval border](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg/250px-The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg)

[Marquess of Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll"), whose [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party") opposed the Engagement

The Scots nominated three Commissioners to negotiate with Charles; [Lauderdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Maitland,_1st_Duke_of_Lauderdale "John Maitland, 1st Duke of Lauderdale"), [Lanark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton,_2nd_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton, 2nd Duke of Hamilton") and [Loudoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Campbell,_1st_Earl_of_Loudoun "John Campbell, 1st Earl of Loudoun"). In December 1647, Charles agreed to impose Presbyterianism in England for three years and suppress the Independents, but his refusal to take the Covenant himself split the Scots.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-10) It was not until April 1648 the Engagers achieved a majority in the [Scottish Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland "Parliament of Scotland"); Argyll's Kirk Party did not trust Charles, objected to an alliance with English and Scots Royalists, and denounced the Engagement as 'sinful.'[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMitchisonFryFry2002223%E2%80%93224-11)

Most of the Scottish army had been demobilised and efforts to recruit new regiments were undermined when many refused to serve, including their most experienced generals, [Lord Leven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Leslie,_1st_Earl_of_Leven "Alexander Leslie, 1st Earl of Leven") and [David Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leslie_(Scottish_general) "David Leslie (Scottish general)"). The inexperienced [Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 1st Duke of Hamilton") was given command, with the [Earl of Callendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Livingston,_1st_Earl_of_Callendar "James Livingston, 1st Earl of Callendar") as his subordinate. When deputy to Leven, Callendar's overestimation of his military abilities had led to constant conflict and this was repeated with Hamilton. His commander of infantry, [William Baillie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Baillie_(soldier) "William Baillie (soldier)"), had direct experience of the New Model Army and doubted their ability to defeat it.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005424-12)

After dispersing Kirk Party dissidents at [Mauchline Muir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir "Battle of Mauchline Muir") in June 1648, a poorly trained Engager army of 9,000 marched into England. The [Second English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War "Second English Civil War") was intended as a series of Royalist risings in England and Wales, with the Scots providing support. By the time Hamilton's army entered [Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire") in early August, the other revolts had been suppressed and Cromwell routed the Engagers at [Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Preston_(1648) "Battle of Preston (1648)") on 19 August. Hamilton was taken prisoner and executed in March 1649.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005470-13)

Defeat at Preston led to the collapse of the Engager regime; the Kirk Party took control of [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") and although repulsed at [Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stirling_(1648) "Battle of Stirling (1648)") in September, a new civil war seemed imminent. However, with Cromwell's support, Argyll took control and expelled his Engager opponents, with English troops being withdrawn.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005470-13)

The 1649 [Act of Classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Act_of_Classes "Act of Classes") banned Engagers and Royalists from holding political or military office and established the Kirk Party as the government of Scotland. However, the execution of Charles in January 1649 was viewed by Covenanters as an offence against God; they proclaimed his son [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") King of Scotland and Great Britain. In the 1650 [Treaty of Breda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Breda_(1650) "Treaty of Breda (1650)"), they agreed to restore Charles to the English throne; in return he accepted the Covenant. Defeats by Cromwell at [Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dunbar_(1650) "Battle of Dunbar (1650)") and [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Worcester "Battle of Worcester") resulted in Scotland being incorporated into the [Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England,_Scotland_and_Ireland "Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland") in 1654.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005520-14)

12.title: Reformation History
12.content:
During the years between 1647 and 1651 the Covenanters were in control in Scotland, but also became divided because of a number of disagreements over their attitude to king [Charles’](https://reformationhistory.org/charlesI.html) son, [Charles II](https://reformationhistory.org/charlesII.html).

In 1645, Charles I had been finally defeated by [Oliver Cromwell](https://reformationhistory.org/olivercromwell.html) and became a prisoner of the English Parliament. On 26 December 1647 some of the Scottish nobles secretly visited Charles and promised that they would raise an army in Scotland to attack England if he would allow Presbyterianism to be set up for three years. This agreement, known as the Engagement, was agreed to by the Scottish Parliament, but the General Assembly weren’t happy with it. The army raised to fight the English was soon defeated at Preston in 1648.

Following this, the strict Covenanters gained control of Parliament and in January 1649 they passed the Act of Classes which removed those who had taken part in the Engagement from the army and from important jobs. A week later however, the English Parliament executed Charles I. Although the Covenanters had disagreed with Charles, they also disagreed with killing the king, and the Scottish Parliament immediately declared his son, Charles II, who was living in Holland, as the new king. Between the failure of the Engagement in 1648 and the Battle of Dunbar (see below) in 1650, the Covenanters were in control of the government of Scotland. Their rule showed a real concern for the poor and oppressed, and they passed strict laws against injustice and moral sins and witchcraft.

In June 1650, Charles signed the [Solemn League and Covenant](https://reformationhistory.org/solemnleagueandcovenant.html) and landed in Scotland. The English immediately invaded and the Scottish army was soon defeated at Dunbar by Cromwell, who then captured Edinburgh. After this defeat the Parliament and General Assembly accepted the Public Resolutions which let people who had taken part in the Engagement back into the army to fight for Charles II. The Covenanters split into Resolutioners (who agreed with the Public Resolutions) and Protestors (who didn’t). The Resolutioners thought that Scotland’s problems were because of a lack of unity, but the Protestors thought that their problems were because they weren’t seeking Christ first and foremost.

On 1 January 1651, Charles II was crowned King of Scotland at Scone after accepting the covenants and agreeing to set up Presbyterianism. Although a large part of Scotland was in English control, the Scots then invaded England. Again, they were totally defeated. Charles II managed to escape to France.

| Religion | [Presbyterianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism "Presbyterianism") ([Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland")) |
| * [Politics of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Scotland "Politics of Scotland") * [Political parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_Scotland "List of political parties in Scotland") * [Elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Scotland "Elections in Scotland") |

The **Engagers** were a faction of the [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland")[Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters"), who made "**The Engagement**" with King [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") in December 1647 while he was imprisoned in [Carisbrooke Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle") by the [English Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Parliamentarians "English Parliamentarians") after his defeat in the [First Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War").

[![Image 2: A historical document titled A Solemn League and Covenant with text detailing Reformation and defence of Religion, the Honour and happiness of the King, and the Peace and Safety of the three kingdoms of England, Scotland, and Ireland](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/The_Solemn_League_And_Covenant.jpg/250px-The_Solemn_League_And_Covenant.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Solemn_League_And_Covenant.jpg)

The [Solemn League and Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solemn_League_and_Covenant "Solemn League and Covenant") agreed by English and Scottish Presbyterians in 1643

In the 17th and 18th centuries, politics and religion were closely linked; it is impossible to understand differences between Engagers, Royalists or [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party") political views without an appreciation of these distinctions.

'[Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_polity "Presbyterian polity")' versus '[Episcopalian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_polity "Episcopal polity")' implied differences in governance, not [doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctrine "Doctrine"). Episcopalian meant rule by bishops, appointed by the monarch; Presbyterian structures were controlled by [Elders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elder_(Christianity) "Elder (Christianity)"), nominated by their congregations. Arguments over structure or governance of the church were as much about politics and the power of the monarch as religious practice; political divisions often centred on different interpretations of this.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-1)

The [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Reformation "English Reformation") created a [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland"), or 'kirk', Presbyterian in structure and governance, and predominantly [Calvinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinism "Calvinism") in doctrine. When [James VI and I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_VI_and_I "James VI and I") became king of England in 1603, a unified Church of Scotland and England governed by bishops became the first step in his vision of a centralised, Unionist state.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStephen201055%E2%80%9358-2) Although both churches were nominally Episcopalian, they were very different in doctrine; even bishops in Scotland viewed many [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") practices as little better than Catholicism.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonald199875%E2%80%9376-3)

[![Image 3: Painting of Algernon Sidney wearing armor with a white collar](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg/250px-1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg)

[James Graham, Marquis of Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquis_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquis of Montrose"); Royalist commander in Scotland 1644–1645, but a Covenanter general 1638 to 1640

Efforts by [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") to impose uniform practices led to the 1638 [National Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Covenant "National Covenant"), whose signatories pledged to resist liturgical 'innovations'. In December 1638, bishops were expelled from the kirk; when Charles attempted to use military force, he was defeated in the 1639 and 1640 [Bishops' Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops%27_Wars "Bishops' Wars"), which left the [Covenanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanter "Covenanter") party in control of Scotland.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMackieLenmanParker1986204%E2%80%93205-4)

Calvinists believed a 'well-ordered' monarchy was part of God's plan; as a result, the vast majority of Covenanters agreed monarchy itself was divinely ordered but disagreed on who held ultimate authority in clerical affairs.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacleod20095%E2%80%9319_passim-5) Royalists and Engagers tended to argue the king held supreme authority, but that did not necessarily mean they supported bishops and individual motives were very complex. Many fought for both Covenant and king at different times, including [Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquis_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquis of Montrose").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris201553%E2%80%9354-6)

When the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") began in 1642, Scotland initially remained neutral, but became involved in the [Irish Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Rebellion_of_1641 "Irish Rebellion of 1641"); the bitterness of this conflict radicalised views in Scotland and Ireland.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005142-7) The Covenanter faction known as the [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party"), led by [Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll"), saw religious union with England as the best way to preserve a Presbyterian kirk and in October 1643 the [Solemn League and Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solemn_League_and_Covenant "Solemn League and Covenant") agreed a Presbyterian Union in return for Scottish military support.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobertson2014125-8)

Royalists and moderates in both Scotland and England opposed union, as did the religious [Independents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_(religion) "Independent (religion)") like [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell"), who dominated the [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") and opposed any state-ordered church. Both Covenanters and their English allies saw the Independents as a bigger threat than the Royalists and when Charles surrendered in 1646, they began negotiations to restore him to the English throne.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005420%C2%B7423-9)

[![Image 4: Portrait of Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll, depicting a man in a black cap and dark clothing with a white collar, set against a plain background and framed within an oval border](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg/250px-The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg)

[Marquess of Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll"), whose [Kirk Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party") opposed the Engagement

The Scots nominated three Commissioners to negotiate with Charles; [Lauderdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Maitland,_1st_Duke_of_Lauderdale "John Maitland, 1st Duke of Lauderdale"), [Lanark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton,_2nd_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton, 2nd Duke of Hamilton") and [Loudoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Campbell,_1st_Earl_of_Loudoun "John Campbell, 1st Earl of Loudoun"). In December 1647, Charles agreed to impose Presbyterianism in England for three years and suppress the Independents, but his refusal to take the Covenant himself split the Scots.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-10) It was not until April 1648 the Engagers achieved a majority in the [Scottish Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland "Parliament of Scotland"); Argyll's Kirk Party did not trust Charles, objected to an alliance with English and Scots Royalists, and denounced the Engagement as 'sinful.'[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMitchisonFryFry2002223%E2%80%93224-11)

Most of the Scottish army had been demobilised and efforts to recruit new regiments were undermined when many refused to serve, including their most experienced generals, [Lord Leven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Leslie,_1st_Earl_of_Leven "Alexander Leslie, 1st Earl of Leven") and [David Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leslie_(Scottish_general) "David Leslie (Scottish general)"). The inexperienced [Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 1st Duke of Hamilton") was given command, with the [Earl of Callendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Livingston,_1st_Earl_of_Callendar "James Livingston, 1st Earl of Callendar") as his subordinate. When deputy to Leven, Callendar's overestimation of his military abilities had led to constant conflict and this was repeated with Hamilton. His commander of infantry, [William Baillie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Baillie_(soldier) "William Baillie (soldier)"), had direct experience of the New Model Army and doubted their ability to defeat it.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005424-12)

After dispersing Kirk Party dissidents at [Mauchline Muir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir "Battle of Mauchline Muir") in June 1648, a poorly trained Engager army of 9,000 marched into England. The [Second English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War "Second English Civil War") was intended as a series of Royalist risings in England and Wales, with the Scots providing support. By the time Hamilton's army entered [Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire") in early August, the other revolts had been suppressed and Cromwell routed the Engagers at [Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Preston_(1648) "Battle of Preston (1648)") on 19 August. Hamilton was taken prisoner and executed in March 1649.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005470-13)

Defeat at Preston led to the collapse of the Engager regime; the Kirk Party took control of [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") and although repulsed at [Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stirling_(1648) "Battle of Stirling (1648)") in September, a new civil war seemed imminent. However, with Cromwell's support, Argyll took control and expelled his Engager opponents, with English troops being withdrawn.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005470-13)

The 1649 [Act of Classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Act_of_Classes "Act of Classes") banned Engagers and Royalists from holding political or military office and established the Kirk Party as the government of Scotland. However, the execution of Charles in January 1649 was viewed by Covenanters as an offence against God; they proclaimed his son [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") King of Scotland and Great Britain. In the 1650 [Treaty of Breda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Breda_(1650) "Treaty of Breda (1650)"), they agreed to restore Charles to the English throne; in return he accepted the Covenant. Defeats by Cromwell at [Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dunbar_(1650) "Battle of Dunbar (1650)") and [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Worcester "Battle of Worcester") resulted in Scotland being incorporated into the [Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England,_Scotland_and_Ireland "Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland") in 1654.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005520-14)

15.title: Battle of Preston – The decisive end of the Civil War
15.content:
This engagement marked the decisive close to the [Second English Civil War](https://sevenswords.uk/english-civil-war-every-battle/). [Oliver Cromwell’s](https://sevenswords.uk/oliver-cromwell/) New Model Army faced a combined Royalist force, largely Scottish Engagers, in a pursuit that turned into a rout and sealed the fate of the militarised uprising.

### Background

[Charles I](https://sevenswords.uk/charles-i-of-england/) had sought to regain his throne by negotiating with a faction of Scots, known as the Engagers, who agreed to assist him in return for ecclesiastical concessions. In response, Cromwell marched north and met Hamilton’s army around Preston.

According to contemporary accounts, “[in] one skirmish the commander of their advance guard was killed,” underlining the fierce resistance Cromwell faced even in pursuit.

* * *

Forces
------

### Leaders

**Parliamentarians (New Model Army / Northern Association / Lancashire Militia)**

*   Oliver Cromwell commanded the main New Model Army.
*   John Lambert led Northern Association forces.
*   Regional militia under various local commanders.

**Royalists (Scottish Engagers with English Royalist support)**

*   Duke of Hamilton led the main Scottish Engager army.
*   General William Baillie oversaw the infantry contingent.
*   Lords Langdale and Musgrave commanded Royalist English elements.

### Troop Composition

| Side | Infantry | Cavalry | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Parliamentarians | ~5,300 | ~3,700 | Figures include New Model, Lambert’s forces, and militia |
| Royalists | ~18,300 (Scottish) + ~4,500 (Royalist) | ~5,700 total | Not all were engaged; many units understrength |

A contemporary voice, likely exaggerating but telling in tone, claimed “not a fifth man could handle a pike,” a comment aimed at the poor training and morale of many Scottish troops.

* * *

Arms and Armour
---------------

Infantry were organised into regiments of musketeers and pikemen. Musketeers used four-foot, matchlock muskets, with some flintlock variants, while pikemen wielded 15–18-foot pikes, often bearing body armour and helmets.

Cavalry on both sides wore pot helmets, thigh-length boots and cuirasses or leather jerkins. Parliamentarian horsemen typically carried two pistols and a sword, their flintlocks offering better reliability in rain. Scots often bore lances instead of pistols, useful in open warfare but clumsy in Preston’s broken terrain.

Dragoons had become specialised mounted troops by 1648, some using carbines, while the Scots still clung to older matchlock muskets.

At the Battle of Preston in August 1648, the types of swords in use reflected the mixed composition of the armies and the transitional nature of mid-17th-century warfare. While firearms, pikes, and polearms dominated the battlefield, swords were still an essential sidearm for officers, cavalry, and some infantry.

**Parliamentarian New Model Army and Northern Association forces**

*   **[Mortuary swords](https://sevenswords.uk/the-mortuary-sword/)**: A distinctly English cavalry weapon, with a broad, double-edged blade, basket hilt, and decorative pommel often bearing a portrait mask. Common among Parliamentarian officers and troopers.
*   **Baskethilt broadswords**: These were increasingly common for both horse and foot soldiers, offering hand protection in close combat.
*   **[Rapiers](https://sevenswords.uk/rapier/)**: Mostly carried by officers and gentlemen; long, slender, and more suited to duelling or command presence than mass battle.
*   **[Hangers](https://sevenswords.uk/hanger-sword/)**: Short, curved blades often worn by dragoons or militia for camp defence and as a secondary weapon.

**Royalist Scottish Engager and English Royalist forces**

*   **[Scottish baskethilt broadswords](https://sevenswords.uk/scottish-basket-hilt-broadsword/)**: Sometimes called “claymores” in this period (the single-handed type, not the later two-handed highland sword). These were robust, double-edged, and ideal for hacking in close quarters.
*   **Mortuary swords**: Carried by many English Royalist cavalrymen, similar to those of the Parliamentarians.
*   **Rapiers**: Present among officers, especially in the English Royalist contingents.
*   **[Dirks](https://sevenswords.uk/scottish-dirk-the-highland-warrior-blade/) and daggers**: Secondary blades often carried by Scots alongside their broadswords.

Although pikes and muskets were the primary arms of infantry, when formations collapsed—such as in the close fighting at Ribbleton Moor and Winwick—these swords became decisive in the hand-to-hand engagements.

* * *

Archaeology
-----------

No major modern excavations of the battlefield are recorded in mainstream sources, so physical evidence remains largely in local museums, such as the Warrington Museum, which houses artefacts like musket balls and possibly frame-gun shot dating from the conflict. These finds hint at the intense close-quarters fighting, especially around Walton and Winwick.

* * *

Battle Timeline
---------------

![Image 1: Battle of Preston map displays the movement of the Royalist and Parliamentarian armies from 17-19 August 1648](https://sevenswords.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/battle-map-Preston.jpg)
**17 August**

Cromwell surprised Hamilton’s scattered forces around Ribbleton Moor. Langdale’s infantry formed a defensive line that held off Parliamentarian cavalry with pikemen. After fierce combat, what Cromwell termed “a very stiff and sturdy resistance,” Parliamentarian infantry and local militia cracked the line and swept toward the Ribble bridge, forcing a breakthrough.

**Evening of 17 August**

Thousands of Scots were captured as fields became littered with prisoners. Royalists regrouped south of the river as Parliamentarians secured the bridge and surrounding approaches. Cromwell declared the enemy “broken” in a letter.

**18 August**

The Scots escaped south in the night, abandoning artillery, baggage and ammunition. The Parliamentarians pressed on relentlessly, catching and disrupting the retreat.

**19 August (Battle of Winwick)**

Exhausted but cornered, the Scots halted near Winwick. Fierce fighting ensued. Parliamentarian cavalry pinned Scots in place while infantry attacked from the flanks. Formations broke and many fled into the church at Winwick, where they surrendered. The Scottish cavalry slipped away but many surrendered in Warrington and Uttoxeter soon after.

* * *

Contemporary Reflections
------------------------

Cromwell estimated “2,000 Royalists were killed and 9,000 captured,” though historians suggest such figures are inflated. Modern estimates put Royalist deaths around 1,000 at Preston, with 4,000 prisoners; the broader campaign, including Winwick, added about 1,000 killed and 7,000–8,000 taken prisoner.

One Scots officer, overwhelmed, “beseeched any that would to shoot him through the head,” a vivid testament to the despair of the defeated leadership.

* * *

Aftermath and Perspective
-------------------------

The battle effectively ended organised Scottish military support for the Royalists in this war. Hundreds of prisoners were sold or pressed into service overseas. Hamilton was subsequently beheaded. The execution of Charles I followed not long after. England became a republic under the Commonwealth, while Scotland ultimately fell under Cromwell’s rule.

December 21: An important update for readers in the United States. 

You deserve an explanation, so please don't skip this 1-minute read. It's Sunday, December 21. Fewer people are seeing our message this month so it's harder than ever to hit our goal. If you've lost count of how many times you've visited Wikipedia this year, we hope that means it's given you at least $2.75 of knowledge. If everyone who finds Wikipedia useful gave $2.75, we'd hit our goal in a few hours.

It's been 25 years and Wikipedia is still free. It's still created by people, not machines, and we don't run ads or put up paywalls because we're not here to make a profit off your attention. In other words, it's still the internet we were promised.

Less than 2% of our readers donate, so if you have given in the past and Wikipedia still provides you with $2.75 worth of knowledge, donate today. If you are undecided, remember any contribution helps.

Where your donation goes

 Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://annual.wikimedia.org/) for more information about our financial health. 

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

34% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

11% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 
Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

**James Hamilton, 1st Duke of Hamilton** (19 June 1606 – 9 March 1649), known as **the 3rd Marquess of Hamilton** from March 1625 until April 1643, was a [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Scotland "Kingdom of Scotland") nobleman and influential political and military leader during the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War "Thirty Years' War") and the [Wars of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms").

James was born in 1606 at [Hamilton Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_Palace "Hamilton Palace") in [Lanarkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanarkshire "Lanarkshire"), the son of [James, 2nd Marquess of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_2nd_Marquess_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 2nd Marquess of Hamilton"), and the [Lady Ann Cunningham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Ann_Cunningham "Lady Ann Cunningham"), daughter of [James, 7th Earl of Glencairn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cunningham,_7th_Earl_of_Glencairn "James Cunningham, 7th Earl of Glencairn"). Following the death of his insane great-uncle [James, Earl of Arran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_3rd_Earl_of_Arran "James Hamilton, 3rd Earl of Arran"), in 1609, the infant was styled [Earl of Arran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Arran_(Scotland) "Earl of Arran (Scotland)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-1)

### Heir to the throne of Scotland

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Heir to the throne of Scotland")]

The young Earl of Arran's close ancestor was the Princess Mary, daughter to [James II of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_Scotland "James II of Scotland") and [Mary of Guelders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_of_Guelders "Mary of Guelders"). After the death in 1612 of [Henry Frederick, Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Frederick,_Prince_of_Wales "Henry Frederick, Prince of Wales"), James became third in line to the throne of Scotland, after [Charles, Duke of Rothesay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"), and his sister [Elizabeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Stuart,_Queen_of_Bohemia "Elizabeth Stuart, Queen of Bohemia").

James VI's first visit to Scotland since the [Union of the Crowns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_the_Crowns "Union of the Crowns") occurred in early 1617, while in Scotland, he was apparently charmed by [The 2nd Marquess of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_2nd_Marquess_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 2nd Marquess of Hamilton"), and invited him to court in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"). The [Marquess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquess "Marquess") duly arrived in London in August of that year, with his eleven-year-old son, Lord Arran. Although like most noblemen's sons of the time he had a private tutor, James Bale, Arran's time spent at court in the ensuing years did not consist of much formal education.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] To remedy this, Arran was sent to [Exeter College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeter_College,_Oxford "Exeter College, Oxford"); he matriculated on 14 December 1621.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2)

The future 1st Duke of Hamilton was interested in art from a young age and collected Venetian paintings through his agent [Viscount Basil Feilding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_Feilding,_2nd_Earl_of_Denbigh "Basil Feilding, 2nd Earl of Denbigh").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-jstor-3) An inventory of his collection was made sometime after [Charles I's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") retreat from London in November 1642 and before 12 April 1643, which included 600 entries, of which half were Venetian paintings from the collections of [Bartolomeo della Nave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomeo_della_Nave "Bartolomeo della Nave") and others.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-jstor-3) A good portion of this collection later came into the hands of the [Archduke Leopold Wilhelm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archduke_Leopold_Wilhelm "Archduke Leopold Wilhelm") in Brussels and forms a key part of the collection of the [Kunsthistorisches Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsthistorisches_Museum "Kunsthistorisches Museum") in [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna") today.

The Marquess meanwhile had been intriguing with [George, 1st Duke of Buckingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Villiers,_1st_Duke_of_Buckingham "George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham"). Like all ambitious upstarts at court, Buckingham was keen to consolidate his new-found fortunes by allying himself and his family with established and wealthy families. Buckingham proposed to wed Lord Arran to his niece Mary, daughter to [William, Viscount Feilding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Feilding,_1st_Earl_of_Denbigh "William Feilding, 1st Earl of Denbigh"), an undistinguished [Warwickshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwickshire "Warwickshire")[squire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squire "Squire").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Lord Hamilton, despite his misgivings regarding Buckingham's lowly origins, was impressed enough by his influence with the king to accept his suggestion.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] On 16 June 1622, the fifteen-year-old Arran married nine-year-old Mary Feilding in the presence of the king.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Arran was not consulted and later came to bitterly resent it.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Marquess of Hamilton
--------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Marquess of Hamilton")]

[![Image 2: Painting of young man wearing 17th-century dress consisting of bright red hose and a black doublet, holding a black hat and white gloves in his left hand](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Dani%C3%ABl_Mijtens_-_Portrait_of_James_Hamilton%2C_Earl_of_Arran%2C_Later_3rd_Marquis_and_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton%2C_Aged_17_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/250px-Dani%C3%ABl_Mijtens_-_Portrait_of_James_Hamilton%2C_Earl_of_Arran%2C_Later_3rd_Marquis_and_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton%2C_Aged_17_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dani%C3%ABl_Mijtens_-_Portrait_of_James_Hamilton,_Earl_of_Arran,_Later_3rd_Marquis_and_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton,_Aged_17_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)

Portrait by [Daniël Mijtens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani%C3%ABl_Mijtens "Daniël Mijtens") of James, then [Earl of Arran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Arran_(Scotland) "Earl of Arran (Scotland)"), in 1623 (age 17). Painting is owned by [Tate Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Britain "Tate Britain"), London. Lord Arran succeeded as The 3rd Marquess of Hamilton in April 1625.

On 2 March 1625, the 2nd Marquess died[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2) at [Whitehall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehall "Whitehall") of a seizure. His death was blamed on fever, although the speed of his death and his age, thirty-six, made many suspect poison.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] King James died three weeks later. The new 3rd Marquess of Hamilton, as Lord Arran now became, received all his father's titles, and also the same annuity his father had received from the court of £2,500 sterling. At the coronation of King [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"), young Lord Hamilton bore the [Sword of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword_of_State "Sword of State") at [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-4)

In 1628, Lord Hamilton was made a [Gentleman of the Bedchamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentleman_of_the_Bedchamber "Gentleman of the Bedchamber"), [Knight of the Garter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_of_the_Garter "Knight of the Garter"), a privy counsellor in both England and Scotland, and in the same year was made [Master of the Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_the_Horse "Master of the Horse"), a post he stayed in until 1644.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-5) He represented the [King of Bohemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_III,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand III, Holy Roman Emperor") at the baptism of the infant Prince Charles.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-6)

Hamilton's army in Germany
--------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Hamilton's army in Germany")]

In 1631 Hamilton took over an army to assist [Gustavus Adolphus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavus_Adolphus "Gustavus Adolphus") in the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War "Thirty Years' War") in Germany.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-7) He raised these based on warrants to levy 6,000 men in England and a further 6,000 in Scotland. There has been much historical debate as to how many men landed initially, how many served in total and how effective these were. What is now known is that the initial contingent of 8,000 landed in Germany and other regiments, such as those of Sir Frederick Hamilton and Alexander Lord Forbes which were raised on warrants designed for the Marquis, actually arrived in Germany but served in the army group of Swedish commander [Åke Tott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%85ke_Tott "Åke Tott").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-8)

Having no military training, Hamilton was assigned Major General [Alexander Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Leslie "Alexander Leslie") as his mentor and other Scottish officers after Leslie was wounded. The command structure of the Hamilton Army was largely Scottish and was drawn from a mix of existing Scottish commanders in Swedish service. Major General Alexander Leslie and 'Dear Sandy' Alexander Hamilton (General of Artillery) were to be supported by Lieutenant General Archibald Douglas, also of the artillery. Although collectively these men believed they served in the "Scots Army", Marquis Hamilton actually took the title of "General of British" from the existing commander with that title, General [James Spens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Spens_(diplomat) "James Spens (diplomat)") who confusingly was compensated with the title "General of Scots" thereafter.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-9)

Despite being under-resourced, Hamilton's forces did greater service than they are usually given credit for. Under-clothed, and lightly armed, they lost many men to disease early on, but those who survived did very well. They guarded the river [Oder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oder "Oder") while Gustavus Adolphus fought [Tilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Tserclaes,_Count_of_Tilly "Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly") at the [Battle of Breitenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Breitenfeld_(1631) "Battle of Breitenfeld (1631)"). Thereafter Hamilton's army linked up with that of the Swedish field marshal, [Johan Banér](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Ban%C3%A9r "Johan Banér"), and the combined force attacked Magdeburg. To Hamilton's chagrin, Banér wished to retire from the siege due to the cold and his response shows that even though not an experienced soldier, Hamilton was not without courage and made his feelings on the subject abundantly clear to Banér:

> your propositioun of the retiring of my trups in respeckt of the could is so preiuditial to me, both in regard of his Majesties strik commands (which was to dou my best for the attackting of Madeburg) and my oune reputatioun as I had rader lous my lyf as faill in the performans of the woon, or in the leaist degri hazard the lousing of the other, and beliue me, so long as there is wone man before this toun (unless the King Majestie countermanding) I ame fully resolued not to budge from itt, being both myself, offisars and remnant soiours most willing and I hoope as abill to indoure whatsoeuer extremati of could or whatt eals may befall, for the aduansment of his Majesties saruis[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-10)

Thereafter the two armies split. Never being allowed to unite all the regiments he had raised into one single force, many of his regiments continued to fight in other theatres of the Thirty Years' War. Moreover, having been caught up in a serious dispute with the Swedish king, the marquis and many of his officers were discharged from service on 22 October 1632. He returned to Britain taking with him Sir [James Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Hamilton_of_Priestfield&action=edit&redlink=1 "James Hamilton of Priestfield (page does not exist)") of Priestfield, Colonel James Ramsay 'the fair' and Colonel John Hamilton along with a cohort of Scots.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-11) Numerous others of the Hamilton army remained in Swedish service, not least generals Alexander Hamilton and Alexander Leslie, but also numerous of the lesser officers and the surviving common soldiers.

Hamilton and Scotland
---------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Hamilton and Scotland")]

On his return to [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain "Great Britain"), Hamilton became [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England")'s chief adviser in Scottish affairs. In May 1638, after the outbreak of the revolt against the new Prayer-Book, he was appointed commissioner for Scotland to appease the discontents. He described the Covenanters as being "possessed by the devil",[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2) and instead of doing his utmost to support the king's interests is said to have been easily intimidated by the [covenanting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters") leaders. Nevertheless, on 27 July 1638 Charles sent Hamilton back to Scotland with new proposals for the election of an assembly and a [parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland "Parliament of Scotland"), episcopacy being safeguarded but bishops being made responsible to future assemblies. After a wrangle concerning the mode of election he again returned to Charles. Having been sent back to [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") on 17 September 1638, he brought with him a revocation of the prayer-book and canons and another covenant to be substituted for the national covenant. On 21 November 1638, Lord Hamilton presided over the first meeting of the assembly in [Glasgow Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow_Cathedral "Glasgow Cathedral"), but dissolved it on 28 November 1638 on its declaring the bishops responsible to its authority. The assembly, however, continued to sit notwithstanding, and Hamilton returned to England to give an account of his failure, leaving the enemy triumphant and in possession.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2)

[War was now decided upon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops%27_Wars "Bishops' Wars"), and Hamilton was chosen to command an expedition to the [Firth of Forth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firth_of_Forth "Firth of Forth") to menace the rear of the Covenanters. However, he now faced his former military mentor [Alexander Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Leslie "Alexander Leslie"), and the artillery specialist, Alexander Hamilton. Realising the strength of his opposition when he arrived in the Forth on 1 May 1639, he found Royalists had seriously underestimated their opposition. This included his own mother, [Anne, Dowager Marchioness of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Ann_Cunningham "Lady Ann Cunningham"), who served as a colonel in the Army of the Covenant and was said to have threatened to shoot her son dead if he landed his forces in Scotland.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-12) A correspondent wrote, "She goeth in armour and with a pistoll by her side readie charged, and wishes him there, saying shee would burie the bullets in his bowells."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-13)

Whatever prompted his hesitance, the proposed plan to land proved impossible and Hamilton was recalled in June. On 8 July 1639, after a hostile reception at Edinburgh, he resigned his commissionership. He supported [The 1st Earl of Strafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Wentworth,_1st_Earl_of_Strafford "Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford")'s proposal to call the [Short Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_Parliament "Short Parliament"), but otherwise opposed him as strongly as he could, as the chief adversary of the Scots; and he aided [Henry Vane the Elder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Vane_the_Elder "Henry Vane the Elder"), it was believed, in accomplishing Strafford's destruction by sending for him to the [Long Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Parliament "Long Parliament").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2)

Hamilton now supported the parliamentary party, desired an alliance with his nation, and persuaded Charles in February 1641 to admit some of their leaders into the council. On the death of Strafford (12 May 1641) Hamilton was confronted by a new antagonist in [The 5th Earl of Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_1st_Marquess_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquess of Montrose"), who detested both his character and policy and repudiated his supremacy in Scotland.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2)

On 10 August 1641 Hamilton accompanied Charles on his last visit to Scotland. His aim now was to effect an alliance between the king and [Archibald Campbell, 8th Earl of Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll"), the former accepting [Presbyterianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian") and receiving the help of the Scots against the English parliament, and when this failed he abandoned Charles and adhered to Argyll. In consequence he received a challenge from [Lord Ker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kerr,_1st_Earl_of_Lothian "William Kerr, 1st Earl of Lothian"), of which he gave the king information, and obtained from Ker an apology. Montrose wrote to Charles declaring he could prove Hamilton to be a traitor. The king himself spoke of him as being "very active in his own preservation".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2)

Shortly afterwards the plot—known as [The Incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Incident_(conspiracy) "The Incident (conspiracy)")—to seize Argyll, Hamilton and the latter's brother, [William Hamilton, Earl of Lanark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton,_2nd_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton, 2nd Duke of Hamilton"), was discovered, and on 12 October 1641 they fled from Edinburgh. Hamilton returned not long afterwards, and notwithstanding all that had occurred still retained Charles's favour and confidence. He returned with him to London and accompanied him on 5 January 1642 when he went to the city after [the failure to secure the five members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Members "Five Members").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2) In July that year Hamilton went to Scotland on a hopeless mission to prevent the intervention of the Scots in the impending [English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War"), and a breach then took place between him and Argyll.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2)

Duke of Hamilton, and execution
-------------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Duke of Hamilton, and execution")]

[![Image 3: Coat of arms that are divided in four. In the top left and bottom right parts, there are three white flowers on a red background. In the other parts, there is a black vessel on a white background. The coat of arms has a crown with red and gold jewels on top](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Coat_of_arms_of_Sir_James_Hamilton%2C_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton%2C_KG.png/250px-Coat_of_arms_of_Sir_James_Hamilton%2C_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton%2C_KG.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coat_of_arms_of_Sir_James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton,_KG.png)

Arms of James, Duke of Hamilton

On 12 April 1643, Hamilton was further ennobled. At Oxford, King Charles conferred upon the Marquess the titles of **Duke of Hamilton**, **Marquess of Clydesdale**, **Earl of Cambridge**, the **Baron of Aven and Innerdale**; in addition he also regranted the Earldom of Arran.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBalfour_Paul1907377-14)

Earlier, in February 1643, proposals of mediation between Charles and Parliament came from Scotland, Hamilton instigated the "cross petition" which demanded from Charles the surrender of the annuities of tithes in order to embarrass [the 1st Earl of Loudoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Campbell,_1st_Earl_of_Loudoun "John Campbell, 1st Earl of Loudoun"), the chief promoter of the project, to whom they had already been granted. This failing, he promoted a scheme for overwhelming the influence and votes of Argyll and his party by sending to Scotland all the Scottish peers then with the king, thereby preventing any assistance to Parliament coming from that quarter, while Charles was to guarantee the establishment of Presbyterianism in Scotland only. This intrigue was strongly opposed by Montrose, who was eager to strike a sudden blow and anticipate and annihilate the plans of the Covenanters. Hamilton, however, gained over the queen, [Henrietta Maria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta_Maria "Henrietta Maria"), for his project, while Montrose was condemned to inaction. Hamilton's scheme, however, completely failed. He had no control over the parliament. He was unable to hinder the meeting of the convention of the [estates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estates_of_the_realm "Estates of the realm") which assembled without the king's authority, and his supporters found themselves in a minority.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2)

Finally, on refusing to take the Covenant, Hamilton and Lanark were obliged to leave Scotland. They arrived at Oxford on 16 December 1643. The Duke of Hamilton's conduct had at last incurred Charles's resentment and he was imprisoned in the house of a baker called Daniells, with only two servants and not allowed to leave the house. He was sent, in January 1644, a prisoner to [Pendennis Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pendennis_Castle "Pendennis Castle"), in 1645 being removed to [St Michael's Mount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Michael%27s_Mount "St Michael's Mount"), where he was liberated by [Lord Fairfax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Fairfax "Thomas Fairfax")'s troops on 23 April 1646.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2)

In 1646, Charles conferred on the Duke the heritable office of [Keeper of Holyroodhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holyrood_Palace "Holyrood Palace").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-15)

Subsequently, he showed great activity in the futile negotiations between the Scots and Charles at [Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne"). In 1648, in consequence of the seizure of Charles by the army in 1647, Hamilton obtained a temporary influence and authority in the [Parliament of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland "Parliament of Scotland") over Argyll, and led a large force into England in support of the king on 8 July 1648. He showed complete incapacity in military command; was kept in check for some time by [John Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lambert_(general) "John Lambert (general)"); and though outnumbering the enemy by 24,000 to about 9,000 men, allowed his troops to disperse over the country and to be [defeated in detail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defeat_in_detail "Defeat in detail") by [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") during the three days 17–19 August 1648 at the [Battle of Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Preston_(1648) "Battle of Preston (1648)"), being himself taken prisoner on 25 August. He was tried on 6 February 1649, condemned to death on 6 March and executed by [decapitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decapitation "Decapitation") on 9 March.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2)

Character assessment
--------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Character assessment")]

Hamilton, during his unfortunate career, had often been suspected of betraying the king's cause, and, as an heir to the Scottish throne, of intentionally playing into the hands of the Covenanters with a view of procuring the Crown for himself.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886-2)

The charge was brought against him as early as 1631 when he was levying men in Scotland for the German expedition, but Charles gave no credence to it and showed his trust in the then-3rd Marquess of Hamilton by causing him to share his own room. The charge, however, always clung to him, and his intriguing character and hopeless management of the king's affairs in Scotland gave colour to the accusation. There seems, however, to be no real foundation for it. His career is sufficiently explained by his thoroughly [egotistical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egotistical "Egotistical") character. Usually Hamilton is thought to have taken no interest whatever in the great questions at issue, and was neither loyal nor [patriotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriotic "Patriotic"), and only desired peace and compromise to avoid personal losses.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYorke1911886%E2%80%93887-16) It has been said that "He was devoid of intellectual or moral strength, and was therefore easily brought to fancy all future tasks easy and all present obstacles insuperable".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGardiner1890179-17)

Issue and succession
--------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Issue and succession")]

[![Image 4: Portrait of Henrietta Anne Stuart, Duchess of Orléans, depicted with long wavy hair adorned with ribbons, wearing a blue gown with a fur stole and pearl jewelry, in front of a column and draped curtain](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Lady_Margaret_Feilding%2C_Duchess_of_Hamilton_by_Henry_Pierce_Bone_after_Anthony_van_Dyck.jpg/250px-Lady_Margaret_Feilding%2C_Duchess_of_Hamilton_by_Henry_Pierce_Bone_after_Anthony_van_Dyck.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lady_Margaret_Feilding,_Duchess_of_Hamilton_by_Henry_Pierce_Bone_after_Anthony_van_Dyck.jpg)

Lady Margaret (or 'Mary') Feilding, Duchess of Hamilton ([Henry Pierce Bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Pierce_Bone "Henry Pierce Bone") after [Anthony van Dyck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_van_Dyck "Anthony van Dyck"))

By his wife Mary Feilding, Hamilton had six children, of whom four died in childhood.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGardiner1890183-18)

*   Henrietta Mary (1631–1632)
*   [Anne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Hamilton,_3rd_Duchess_of_Hamilton "Anne Hamilton, 3rd Duchess of Hamilton") (1632–1716), later _[suo jure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suo\_jure "Suo jure")_ Duchess of Hamilton
*   Susannah (1633–1694), married [The 7th Earl of Cassilis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kennedy,_7th_Earl_of_Cassilis "John Kennedy, 7th Earl of Cassilis") in 1668
*   Charles, [Earl of Arran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Arran_(Scotland) "Earl of Arran (Scotland)") (ca. 1630 – buried 30 April 1640 in [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"))
*   James (1635–1639)
*   William (1636–1638)

Following the death of his three sons, the dukedom passed by special remainder to his brother, [The 1st Earl of Lanark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton,_2nd_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton, 2nd Duke of Hamilton"). On the latter's death at [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Worcester "Battle of Worcester") in 1651, the Scottish titles reverted to the 1st Duke's eldest daughter, Anne. She married [William, Earl of Selkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hamilton,_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton, Duke of Hamilton"), who was created [Duke of Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton "Duke of Hamilton") for life.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGardiner1890183-18)
